items.title: Roy Carew Interview, 1964-11-28
items.q: I have a recording that he made of Froggy Moore, and they called it Froggy Moore Blues... All King Oliver ever did was to record Froggy Moore Blues once.

ctx.x: That was some a year ago. See, he was playing with T-Garden's band.

Yes, well I have a recording that he made of Froggy Moore, and they called it Froggy Moore Blues. I don't know, I'm not sweating about that yet. They called it Froggy Moore Blues, and on the outside of the cover, it says this tune, the King Oliver tune, Froggy Moore's blues, so and so and so, went on like that. All King Oliver ever did was to record Froggy Moore Blues once.

items.title: Roy Carew Interview, 1958-Fall
items.q: The interviewee discusses the song 'Froggy Moore' and speculates on its origin, mentioning 'Freddie Moore' only in the context of the interviewer's suggestion and the interviewee's own impression ('that's my impression that somebody... Oh, he's not going to be good for Freddie Moore'). There is no e

ctx.x: Spice Brothers. Spice Brothers. Spice Brothers, yeah. I wondered whether, uh, whether Jelly wrote both variations of the thing. He probably did, if they were very similar.

Well, he, uh, he wrote Frogger. He wrote Froggy Moore. Then he went out west, uh, uh, at least he was in Los Angeles, and, uh, he played it for Spice Brothers, and got hooked up with them, and they, they took part one and part three and wrote, uh, Froggy Moore. Mm-hmm. See? Just used those two parts. Mm-hmm. Then they all came to Chicago and, uh, uh, assigned Froggy Moore to Melrose, and Melrose took the, the second part, the chorus, and wrote, uh, Sweetheart O' Mine. Sweetheart O' Mine. Now I'm having a heck of…
Sounds like he might have been kidding Freddie Moore. Well, he might have been. Because, who pops, he's ever seen Freddie Moore play, or he plays, his eyes pop, buddy.
